{{short description|Measure of association between two binary variables}}

In statistics, '''Yule's ''Y''''', also known as the '''coefficient of colligation''', is a measure of association between two binary variables. The measure was developed by [[George Udny Yule]] in 1912,<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Yule|first1=G. Udny|title=On the Methods of Measuring Association Between Two Attributes| year=1912|journal=Journal of the Royal Statistical Society|volume=75|issue=6|pages=579–652|doi=10.2307/2340126|jstor=2340126|url=https://zenodo.org/record/1449482}}</ref><ref>Michel G. Soete. A new theory on the measurement of association between two binary variables in medical sciences: association can be expressed in a fraction (per unum, percentage, pro mille....) of perfect association (2013), e-article, BoekBoek.be</ref> and should not be confused with [[skewness#Quantile-based measures|Yule's coefficient]] for measuring [[skewness]] based on [[quartiles]].

==Formula==
For a 2×2 table for [[Binary variable|binary variables]] ''U'' and ''V'' with frequencies or proportions

:{| class="wikitable"
! !! ''V'' = 0 !! ''V'' = 1
|-
| ''U'' = 0 || ''a'' || ''b''
|-
| ''U'' = 1 || ''c'' || ''d''
|}

Yule's ''Y'' is given by

:<math>Y = \frac{\sqrt{ad}-\sqrt{bc}}{\sqrt{ad}+\sqrt{bc}}.</math>

Yule's ''Y'' is closely related to the [[odds ratio]] ''OR''&nbsp;=&nbsp;''ad''/(''bc'') as is seen in following formula:

:<math>Y = \frac{\sqrt{OR}-1}{\sqrt{OR}+1}</math>

Yule's ''Y'' varies from −1 to&nbsp;+1. −1&nbsp;reflects total negative [[correlation]], +1&nbsp;reflects perfect positive association while 0 reflects no association at all. These correspond to the values for the more common [[Pearson correlation]].

Yule's ''Y'' is also related to the similar [[Yule's Q|Yule's ''Q'']], which can also be expressed in terms of the odds ratio. ''Q'' and ''Y'' are related by:

:<math>Q = \frac{2Y}{1+Y^2}\ ,</math>
:<math>Y = \frac{1-\sqrt{1-Q^2}}{Q}\ .</math>

==Interpretation==
{{unreferenced section|date=February 2016}}
Yule's ''Y'' gives the fraction of perfect association in per [[Unum (number format)|unum]] (multiplied by 100 it represents this fraction in a more familiar percentage). Indeed, the formula transforms the original 2×2 table in a crosswise symmetric table wherein ''b'' = ''c'' = 1 and ''a'' = ''d'' = {{radic|''OR''}}.

For a crosswise symmetric table with frequencies or proportions ''a'' = ''d'' and ''b'' = ''c'' it is very easy to see that it can be split up in two tables. In such tables association can be measured in a perfectly clear way by dividing (''a'' – ''b'') by (''a'' + ''b''). In transformed tables b has to be substituted by 1 and a by {{radic|''OR''}}. The transformed table has the same degree of association (the same OR) as the original not-crosswise symmetric table. Therefore, the association in asymmetric tables can be measured by Yule's ''Y'', interpreting it in just the same way as with symmetric tables. Of course, Yule's ''Y'' and (''a''&nbsp;−&nbsp;''b'')/(''a''&nbsp;+&nbsp;''b'') give the same result in crosswise symmetric tables, presenting the association as a fraction in both cases. 

Yule's ''Y'' measures association in a substantial, intuitively understandable way and therefore it is the measure of preference to measure association.{{citation needed|date=February 2016}}

==Examples==
The following crosswise symmetric table

:{| class="wikitable"
! !! ''V'' = 0 !! ''V'' = 1
|-
| ''U'' = 0 || 40 || 10
|-
| ''U'' = 1 || 10 || 40
|}

can be split up into two tables:

:{| class="wikitable"
! !! ''V'' = 0 !! ''V'' = 1
|-
| ''U'' = 0 || 10 || 10
|-
| ''U'' = 1 || 10 || 10
|}

and

:{| class="wikitable"
! !! ''V'' = 0 !! ''V'' = 1
|-
| ''U'' = 0 || 30 || 0
|-
| ''U'' = 1 || 0 || 30
|}

It is obvious that the degree of association equals 0.6 per unum (60%).

The following asymmetric table can be transformed in a table with an equal degree of association (the odds ratios of both tables are equal).

:{| class="wikitable"
! !! ''V'' = 0 !! ''V'' = 1
|-
| ''U'' = 0 || 3 || 1
|-
| ''U'' = 1 || 3 || 9
|}

Here follows the transformed table:

:{| class="wikitable"
! !! ''V'' = 0 !! ''V'' = 1
|-
| ''U'' = 0 || 3 || 1
|-
| ''U'' = 1 || 1 || 3
|}

The odds ratios of both tables are equal to&nbsp;9. ''Y''&nbsp;=&nbsp;(3&nbsp;−&nbsp;1)/(3&nbsp;+&nbsp;1)&nbsp;=&nbsp;0.5&nbsp;(50%)
